summary: Describes a way for DHCP servers to tell clients that no IP address is on offer and that the client should not make up an address for itself. It was later updated by RFC 8925.

eli5.summary: Some computers invent their own address when nobody gives them one. This lets the network say please don't, there is no address for you here.

questions: stop ipv4 link-local addresses with dhcp
how to stop ipv4 link-local addresses with dhcp
subtitle: A DHCP option that lets a server tell clients not to invent their own link-local IPv4 address.

tldr.problem: Some operating systems give themselves a link-local IPv4 address when no DHCP server answers. Sites that rely on unknown hosts getting no address do not want that, but DHCP servers were required to stay silent toward hosts they did not know.
tldr.mechanism: A client adds option 116 (Auto-Configure) to its DHCPDISCOVER. A server that wants to forbid auto-configuration answers with a DHCPOFFER for address 0.0.0.0 and the value DoNotAutoConfigure.
tldr.outcome: The client can now tell a network with no administrator from one whose administrator chose to hand out nothing, and it MUST NOT make up an address in the second case. The RFC was later updated by RFC 8925.

today: RFC 2563 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, but it was updated by RFC 8925.

sections.title: The Problem with Silent DHCP Servers
sections.content:
Operating systems increasingly support ad-hoc networks of two or more machines with little user configuration. When no DHCP server answers, some of them choose a link-local IP address that lets them talk only to hosts on the same link, not past a router. The RFC notes that the IPv4 stacks in Win98 and NT5 did this, and that it caused headaches for sites that rely on machines getting no address when the DHCP servers do not know them.

The difficulty is that DHCP requires servers to silently ignore requests from hosts they do not know. A client therefore cannot tell a subnet with no administrator from one whose administrator deliberately offers nothing. The RFC distinguishes three kinds of nodes: one the administrator configures, one on a segment with no administrator, and one on a managed segment where the administrator chooses to give it nothing.
sections.eli5: If nobody answers, some computers just make up a house number for themselves. A school might not want that, but the helper who hands out numbers was told to stay quiet when it does not know you.

sections.title: The Auto-Configure Option
sections.content:
The option has code 116 and length 1, with a one-byte value. Two values are defined: DoNotAutoConfigure is 0 and AutoConfigure is 1.

When a server answers AutoConfigure, the client MAY generate a link-local address if appropriate. When it answers DoNotAutoConfigure, the client MUST NOT generate one, possibly leaving it with no IP address at all.
sections.eli5: It is a single yes-or-no switch in the message. Zero means do not make up an address, one means you may.

sections.title: Client and Server Behavior
sections.content:
A client that can auto-configure MUST include the option, set to AutoConfigure, in its initial DHCPDISCOVER. When a DHCPOFFER arrives with a yiaddr of 0x00000000, the client consults the option. In both cases the offer MUST be ignored. If the value is AutoConfigure, the client MAY generate a link-local address. If it is DoNotAutoConfigure, and no other offer with a valid yiaddr arrives, the client MUST NOT. How long the client waits to collect other offers is implementation dependent.

On the server side, a DHCPDISCOVER is processed as in the DHCP specification. If no address is chosen, the server stays silent when the option is absent. When the option is present and the administrator has disabled auto-configuration for that subnet or client, the server MUST send a DHCPOFFER for address 0x00000000 with the option set to DoNotAutoConfigure. If auto-configuration is allowed on that subnet, the server stays silent as before.
sections.eli5: The computer asks for an address and mentions it knows the rule. If the network answers an empty offer that says do not invent one, the computer stays without an address.

sections.title: Mixed Environments and Other Messages
sections.content:
Old and new software can coexist. If a client sends the option to a server that does not know it, the server responds normally and does not return a value for it, so the client may auto-configure. If a server supports the option but the client does not send it, the server does nothing about it and the client auto-configures if it gets no response. The RFC says this case SHOULD not occur, because any stack that auto-configures MUST implement this option. Empty offers are only sent when the DISCOVER contained the option, so there are no interoperability problems.

The option only affects the initial address selection. Renewals, releases, declines and informs are handled as in the DHCP specification, because a lease or tested address already exists. If a lease expires, the client returns to the INIT state and sends the initial DHCPDISCOVER as before. A server MAY add the Message option to explain why the client may not auto-configure, and a client that receives it MUST pass it on to its administrator.
sections.eli5: Old computers and new ones can share a network without trouble, because the new rule is only used when both sides know about it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: DHCP itself has no authentication or security mechanisms, and its exposures are discussed in section 7 of the DHCP specification. This option adds one more attack: a malicious user on a subnet can answer every DHCP request with a response saying DoNotAutoConfigure. On a network where auto-configuration is required, that stops all clients from choosing an address.
sections.eli5: A prankster could keep shouting do not make up an address, and then nobody on the network could get one.

items.label: DoNotAutoConfigure
items.desc: Client MUST NOT generate a link-local address.

items.label: AutoConfigure
items.desc: Client MAY generate a link-local address if appropriate.
